Twelve incidents, one bridge

Every one of these had a reading before it had a headline.

The evidence existed. It sat in the wrong office, in the wrong unit, in the wrong vocabulary. This is a tool for the person whose job is to make sure it doesn't.

Longest gap
15 months

Flint, 2014–16 · Legionnaires’ disease. County epidemiologists tied the cluster to the river water in October 2014. The public was told on 13 January 2016. 91 confirmed cases, 12 deaths.

The API run

Then every one of their readings went through the running bridge.

A clean database. Every fixture row posted to the real HTTP API, approved or rejected by a named reviewer, evaluated by the policy engine, hash-chained.

Outcomes

Coded, withheld, or refused. The last two are the product working.

With the bridge

Where the first routed alert lands against the public warning

Fixture readings on a calendar, day 0 = the historical public warning

Synthetic values shaped around the published narrative. A ring is a reading that crossed a policy threshold and was routed.

The record holds

Every call, chained. One edit, found.

After the run, one stored Flint lead reading was rewritten directly in SQLite, the way two high-lead samples were dropped in 2015.

After the run
valid

GET /api/v1/provenance/verify recomputed every digest from GENESIS: 328 entries checked, first invalid sequence: none.

After the edit
invalid at #141

0.104 mg/L rewritten to 0.004 mg/L. Verification stopped at entry 141 and named it. The argument moves from “were these samples valid?” to “here is who decided what, and when.”

Two lines to keep honest

The bridge would not have chlorinated a bore, fixed a valve, or stopped a discharge.

It buys response time. The reading, the lab result, the case count already existed. It makes sure they reach the people who can act, in a shape they can read, with a record that cannot be quietly changed.
